question: What did the General Act of Berlin actually allocate, what did the rules it laid down cost the people on the coasts and in the Congo basin, and what does the free record settle about the counts?
claims: The Act signed at Berlin allocates no territory, names no border and no Power's possession; its 2 articles on occupation set rules for future acts on the coasts, and the British government said, with the conference sitting, that territorial claims were not on its agenda.
The rulers whose land the rules reached speak in this record in their own words, and each of them, Witbooi, Lobengula and Menelik, refuses to let a European text stand for his consent.
The Congo's rubber system and the Herero war are in the record from both sides, and on the deaths the record holds counts of unlike things that this thesis states as counts, never as one number.

lines.text: Most people picture the moment they mean by the Scramble for Africa. Fourteen nations leaning over a map in Berlin, dividing a continent with a ruler and a pen.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: That meeting happened. It ran for one hundred and four days. It drew not one border on any map.

lines.speaker: N
lines.text: What came out of it was a rule. A flag, a garrison, and an administration in place would now beat an older claim made by treaty, or by simply getting there first. The actual taking of the continent took the next thirty years, and none of it was done with a pen.

sentences.text: The General Act of the Conference of Berlin was signed at Berlin on 26 February 1885.

Its preamble says the sovereigns met “to regulate the conditions most favourable to the development of trade and civilization in certain regions of Africa”, and to obviate the disputes “which might in future arise from new acts of occupation” on the coast.
With the conference sitting, on 20 November 1884, the Under-Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs told the Commons that “the decision of territorial claims is not among the bases of the Conference”.
The historian Uzoigwe, writing in the UNESCO General History, holds that the view that the conference did not partition Africa “is correct only in the most technical sense”.
This thesis asks what the Act allocated, what the rules it laid down cost the people they reached, and what the free record settles about the counts.
It makes three claims.
First, that the Act allocates no territory and names no border, and that its articles on occupation are rules for future acts on the coasts.
Second, that the rulers whose land those rules reached speak in this record in their own words, and that each refuses to let a European text stand for his consent.

Third, that the Congo's rubber system and the Herero war are in the record from both sides, and that on the deaths the record holds counts of unlike things, which this thesis states as counts and never as one number.

The primary documents this thesis holds were fetched from the Internet Archive's scans of Hertslet's treaty collection and of four parliamentary papers, from the Historic Hansard service, from the German Historical Institute's documentary edition, from the Assemblée nationale's own site and from the Bundestag, and every passage below was sliced from that copy by a script rather than retyped.
The Act is held in the Foreign Office's English translation, article by article; the French text that governs it was not fetched, because Gallica refused this container.

The African voices held in their own words are a Nama chief's letters in Cape Dutch, with renderings marked as this thesis's own that the page never quotes as text, a Matabele king's letters as a Member of Parliament read them to the Commons, an Ethiopian emperor's letter in a Foreign Office translation, and Herero and Congolese witnesses as the British administration and the British consul recorded them, which is the colonisers' record of the colonised and is treated so under Rule A. The German side speaks through its commander's order and, a century on, through the federal parliament's research service; the Free State speaks through its own commission of inquiry.

The scholarship is held only as the passages cited, from two African historians in the UNESCO General History, an Ethiopian journal, a South African journal, a Sheffield manuscript and a Leiden chapter; the standard monographs on the partition and the paywalled articles on the conference and on the Herero war are known here by name alone and are listed under the gaps.

What the record does not hold is listed under the gaps by name, with what was tried, and the largest are the conference's own protocols, the Rudd Concession in its own words, Menelik's circular to the powers, the Reichstag debates on the Herero war, and any Portuguese source.
The German paper's own statement of the limits of counting comes first.

It writes that the pre-war estimates of the Herero rest on missionaries' figures of doubtful reliability and the post-war figures on the German military's prisoner counts, that the estimates for the whole people run from 35,000 to 100,000 before the war and from 14,000 to 25,000 after it, and that at the extremes this yields loss rates of between 29 and 86 per cent.

The Act's preamble names the sovereigns and presidents who sent plenipotentiaries, and says they met on the invitation of the Imperial Government of Germany, in agreement with the Government of the French Republic.

The Act itself lists the documents it combines: a declaration on freedom of trade in the basin of the Congo, a declaration on the slave trade, a declaration on the neutrality of the conventional basin, an act of navigation for the Congo, an act of navigation for the Niger, and a declaration “introducing into international relations certain uniform rules with reference to future occupations on the coast of the African Continent”.

The first article opens the trade of all nations in the basin of the Congo, and defines that basin by the watersheds of the Niari, the Ogowe, the Schari and the Nile on the north and of the Zambesi and the Loge on the south.

Article VI binds the Powers exercising sovereign rights or influence in those territories “to watch over the preservation of the native tribes, and to care for the improvement of the conditions of their moral and material well-being, and to help in suppressing slavery, and especially the slave trade”.
No article names a Power's possession.

sentences.text: Article XXXIV provides that any Power which henceforth takes possession of a tract of land on the coasts of the African Continent, or assumes a protectorate there, shall accompany the act with a notification “addressed to the other Signatory Powers of the present Act, in order to enable them, if need be, to make good any claims of their own”.

Article XXXV has the signatories recognise “the obligation to insure the establishment of authority in regions occupied by them on the coasts of the African Continent sufficient to protect existing rights”.
Both articles speak of the coasts, of future acts, and of the signatories among themselves.

When Jacob Bright asked in the Commons whether the British representative would be instructed to support the claims of Portugal, the Under-Secretary declined to say what the instructions were, said that “a pledge of secrecy has been given by all the Powers” for the proceedings, and repeated that the decision of territorial claims was not among the bases of the conference.

blocks.title: What the General Act allocates, chapter by chapter
blocks.method: The Act's seven chapters, one row per chapter. The articles each chapter holds and its subject are read from the Act's own table of contents (toc) and from each chapter's opening article, which is the extract the row cites; whether any article in the chapter assigns a territory, a border or a place to a named Power is read from the chapter's articles in the fetched copy, of which the opening article is held. allocates is yes or no, read from the chapter's articles; allocates_n is 1 for yes and 0 for no. The result is the sum of allocates_n.
blocks.finding: Of the Act's 7 chapters, 0 allocate a territory, a border or a place to any Power. The 2 articles on occupation, 34 and 35, set rules for future acts of possession on the coasts and the authority a Power must establish there, and name no Power, no border and no place. The one line the Act draws, in Article 1, bounds the basin in which its free-trade rules run, by watersheds, and gives that basin to no one.

sentences.text: Uzoigwe reads the notification article as the doctrine of spheres of influence and Article 35 as “the so-called doctrine of effective occupation that was to make the conquest of Africa such a murderous business”, and writes that by 1885 the broad lines of the final partition had already been drawn.
He also writes that the conference did not partition Africa in the technical sense, and the two readings are set against each other in the disagreements below.

In the Chambre des députés on 28 juillet 1885, Ferry, a former premier, told the deputies that the Berlin conference had just translated into positive law the duty to combat the slave trade, and, over interruptions from the far left and the right, that “les races supérieures ont un droit vis-à-vis des races inférieures”.
The sixth article and Ferry's sentence are the same claim in a treaty and in a speech, and the next three sections test it against what the Powers' own records say was done.

sentences.text: In Mei 1890, Hendrik Witbooi wrote from Hornkrans to Maharero, chief of the Herero, that he had heard from a letter of Goering's that Maharero had given himself into German protection.
He wrote that every chief has his own people and land, over which he alone commands, and that every chief on this earth is only a place-holder of God, answerable to God alone.
He told Maharero “gy zult eeuwig berouw hebben”, that he would have everlasting regret, for giving his land and his right of government into the hands of the white people.

In June of the next year he wrote to a missionary that the Germans told the chiefs of the land to make friendship with them because other strong nations would seize their ground, but that it now looked as if the German was the man who wanted to seize the land.

blocks.creator: Lobengula, King of Matabeleland, in a British record
blocks.text:
HC Deb 09 November 1893 vol 18 cc543-627
British dominions. On October 15, 1889, Lord Knutsford, on a Petition signed by the two Dukes, Mr. Rhodes, Lord Gifford, and others, granted the Charter, by which the Company were empowered to use and retain the full benefit of concessions so far as they were valid, and to acquire, by concession or agreement, rights and jurisdictions for the purpose of government in the lands referred to, subject to the approval of the Secretary of State. He must now explain how this concession was obtained from Lobengula, for it appeared that he had always absolutely denied that he ever granted it on the terms which appeared on the face of the instrument. When Lobengula was told that he had granted a concession of this nature he sent two Indunas to the Cape, with orders (as could be seen on reference to the Blue Book) to discover, first, whether such a place as England existed; and next, whether, if they discovered that such a place did exist, there was such a person as the Queen of England; and if there was such a place and such a Monarch, they were to lay before her the following letter and to ask her advice on the subject:—
"To Her Majesty Queen Victoria, from Lobengula.
"Some time ago a party of white men came into my country, the principal one appearing to be a man named Rudd. They asked me for a place where they could dig for gold, and said they would give me certain things for the right to do so. I told them to bring it to me, and I would see what I would do. A document was read and presented to me for signature. I asked what it contained, and was told that in it were my words and the words of those men. I put my hand to it. About three months after I heard from other sources I had given the right to all the minerals in my country. I called a meeting of my Indunas and of the white men, and demanded a copy of the document. It was proved to me that I had signed away the right to minerals of the whole country to Rudd and his friends. I have since had a meeting of my Indunas, and they will not recognise the paper, as it contains neither my words nor the words of those who got it from me."

sentences.text: In the Commons in November 1893, Labouchere read the letter Lobengula had sent to Queen Victoria after learning what he had signed: “A document was read and presented to me for signature. I asked what it contained, and was told that in it were my words and the words of those men. I put my hand to it. About three months after I heard from other sources I had given the right to all the minerals in my country”.

The Queen's reply, sent by Lord Knutsford, said that Lobengula was the ruler of his country, that the Englishmen who asked leave to dig had not gone with the Queen's authority, and that “A King gives a stranger an ox, not a whole herd of cattle”.
In August the king wrote again: “If the Queen hears that I have given away the whole country it is not so. I have no one in my country who knows how to write”.

The Crown's editor of treaties records the other side of the same exchange in a footnote: an agreement of February 1888 by which Lobengula undertook to make no treaty with any foreign State or Power ceding any part of his country without the sanction of the High Commissioner, and a concession granted on 30 October 1888 to the representatives of the British South Africa Company.
Labouchere told the House that in October, 1889, “without any further communication with Lobengula, the Company's Charter was granted”.
The concession itself is not in this record, so the king's account of the paper and the Company's are known here only as the British recorded both.
The emperor who kept his throne was the most careful of the three with paper.

On 14 May 1897, Menelik wrote to Rodd proposing that in any future misunderstanding between the Amharic and English versions of the treaty they had written, the French translation he enclosed “be the witness between us”, “as I have no interpreter with me who understands the English language well enough to compare the English and Amharic versions”.
An Ethiopian journal puts the battle of Adwa on March 1, 1896, with 11,000 casualties in total and nearly 43% of the Italian forces killed, wounded or missing.

Boahen's reading of the whole generation is that Africans were faced with two options, to surrender their sovereignty or to defend it, and that the great majority of them “did decide to defend their sovereignty and independence”.

The Commons resolved on 20 May 1903 that the Government of the Congo Free State had at its inception “guaranteed to the Powers that its Native subjects should be governed with humanity, and that no trading monopoly or privilege should be permitted within its dominions”, and asked the Government to confer with the other signatories of the Berlin General Act “by virtue of which the Congo Free State exists”.
The words “and both these guarantees having been constantly violated” were in the motion as Samuel moved it and were left out by amendment before the House agreed to it.
Gorst told the House that “The evidence was perfectly overwhelming”.
The consul who went up the river that year had known it before.

At Bolobo, once one of the most important settlements on the south bank of the Upper Congo, the population “in the early days of civilized rule numbered fully 40,000 people”, and was believed to be not more than 7,000 or 8,000.

On the south shore of Stanley Pool, where fully 5,000 Bateke had lived in three towns, the great majority had crossed in one night to the French territory, and not 100 of the original people remained at Leopoldville.

Casement gave sleeping sickness “a prominent place” among the causes of the diminution of life he observed, and wrote that the people attributed their decrease to other causes as well, “and I think principally”, which is the consul's own judgement of what they told him.

The girl the report calls T 7 told him that when the State soldiers came to her village in the afternoon, “they began catching and tying the people, and killed lots of them”, and that she alone of those who ran escaped.

At Lake Mantumba the local official told him that men still came to him whose hands had been cut off by the Government soldiers, and Casement saw two cases himself, one of them “a young lad of 11 or 12 years of age, whose right hand was cut off at the wrist”.

blocks.title: Every count of the Congo's people in the record
blocks.method: Every figure a fetched document gives for a population of the Congo Free State or for its dead, one row per figure, with the document, what the figure counts, and the before and after or the total as the document states them. The consul's counts are of named places; the historian's are of the whole territory as others estimated it. No range is taken across the rows, because a town's people and a territory's dead are not the same quantity. The result is the number of rows.
blocks.finding: The record holds four counts of four different things: one town, Bolobo, from fully 40,000 to 7,000 or 8,000; one shore of Stanley Pool, from fully 5,000 to not 100 at Leopoldville; the maximalist historians' roughly fifty per cent of the whole population; and the reform campaign's estimated 10 million, which Roes reports as Morel's and Hochschild's figure and the agnostics dispute. The two contemporary counts are the consul's, of places he had known before; the two totals are twentieth-century estimates that the one Tier B source held calls contested. Nothing in the primary record counts the whole.
blocks.confidence: moderate: the count of rows is exact, but two of the four figures are estimates reported at second hand by a historian describing a controversy, and the consul's counts are his own recollection of places against a missionary's belief
blocks.against: the consul assigned a prominent place among the causes of the decrease to sleeping sickness (p21), and the Free State's commission put smallpox and sleeping sickness above every other cause (p117), so the counts measure a fall and not a cause; the commission also recorded that the Bateke crossed to the French bank, which is emigration, not death

sentences.text: The Free State's own commission, sent after the report, found that when the prestations were not forthcoming the chiefs were arrested and some inhabitants taken at random, and that “often the women were held as hostages”; the State, it wrote, “has, for a long time, forbidden this practice, but has been unable to suppress it”.
Of the armed overseers it called sentries, the strangers detailed to a village were “by far the worst sort”.

On depopulation it agreed that from Stanley Pool to New Antwerp the banks of the river were almost deserted, and read the river people as having fled the impositions or been scattered rather than destroyed.
It then set every such cause below smallpox and sleeping sickness: “All of these causes of depopulation are secondary in importance”.
The two records agree on the hostages, the sentries and the emptying of the river, and divide on what the people died of.

Ich der große General der Deutschen Soldaten sende diesen Brief
an das Volk der Herero.
Die Herero sind nicht mehr Deutsche Untertanen. Sie haben
gemordet und gestohlen, haben verwundeten Soldaten Ohren und Nasen
und andere Körperteile abgeschnitten und wollen jetzt aus Feigheit
nicht mehr kämpfen. Ich sage dem Volk: Jeder der einen der Kapitäne
an eine meiner Stationen als Gefangenen abliefert, erhält tausend
Mark, wer Samuel Maherero bringt, erhält fünftausend Mark. Das Volk
der Herero muß jedoch das Land verlassen. Wenn das Volk dies nicht
tut, so werde ich es mit dem Groot Rohr [kapholländisch, Geschütz,
Kanone] dazu zwingen.
Innerhalb der Deutschen Grenze wird jeder Herero mit oder ohne
Gewehr, mit oder ohne Vieh erschossen, ich nehme keine Weiber und
keine Kinder mehr auf, treibe sie zu ihrem Volke zurück oder lasse
auch auf sie schießen.
Dies sind meine Worte an das Volk der Herero.
Der große
General des mächtigen Deutschen Kaisers.
Dieser Erlaß ist bei den Appells den Truppen mitzuteilen mit dem
Hinzufügen, daß auch der Truppe, die einen der Kapitäne fängt, die
entsprechende Belohnung zu teil wird, und daß das Schießen auf
Weiber und Kinder so zu verstehen ist, daß über sie hinweggeschossen
wird, um sie zum Laufen zu zwingen. Ich nehme mit Bestimmtheit an,
daß dieser Erlaß dazu führen wird, keine männliche Gefangene mehr zu
machen, aber nicht zu Grausamkeiten gegen Weiber und Kinder
ausartet. Diese werden schon fortlaufen, wenn zweimal über sie
hinweggeschossen wird. Die Truppe wird sich des guten Rufes der
Deutschen Soldaten bewußt bleiben.
Der Kommandeur.
gez. v. Trotha

sentences.text: The order the German commander signed at Osombo-Windhuk on 2 October 1904 reads, in its own German, “Innerhalb der Deutschen Grenze wird jeder Herero mit oder ohne Gewehr, mit oder ohne Vieh erschossen, ich nehme keine Weiber und keine Kinder mehr auf”, which Ciarlo's published translation renders “Any Herero found within the German frontier, with or without a gun, with or without cattle, will be shot. I spare neither women nor children”.

The addendum to the troops says, in that translation, that the shooting at women and children “is to be understood as shooting above their heads”, and that the order will result in “no more male prisoners being taken”.

Gewald's translation of von Estorff has the officer writing that the people could still have been saved and pardoned, that “I suggested this to General von Trotha”, and “but hè wanted their total extermination”.
The Herero causes are in this record as sworn statements taken by the British administration that replaced the German one.

Daniel Kariko, an under-chief, swore that “Our people were compelled to work on farms, and the farmers had them chained up by the police and flogged without mercy for the slightest little thing”, that a German was declared not guilty of murdering a chief's daughter and then given three years on a new trial, and that “This decided us for war”.

Gottlob Kamatoto swore that after messages that the war was over, “seven Herero leaders came into the German camp to discuss peace terms”, and that at sunset “the seven peace envoys were caught and tied with ropes. They were led aside and shot”.
Gerard Kamaheke swore that he went in to Ombakaha with the chiefs Saul and Joel and 70 Herero soldiers, that the Germans opened fire, and that “I lay quite still and pretended to be dead”.

The same report prints the amnesty proclamation of 1st December 1905 that called the survivors in, “Come and lay down your arms, Hereros!”, and told them that Hendrik Witbooi had been killed by a German bullet.
A review in a South African journal records that in 1926 the report was withdrawn from circulation in libraries and archives throughout the British Empire.

blocks.method: Every figure a fetched document gives for the Herero people before and after the war of 1904, one row per figure, with the document, its producer, and the before, after and share as the document states them; where a document gives only a share the counts are blank, and where it gives a range the range is kept. blocks.finding: The record holds four counts of the Herero from three producers, and they do not agree: the British administration's 80,000 to 90,000 reduced to about 15,000; a missionary-quoting historian's no fewer than 80 per cent; a British campaigner of 1949, as the same historian quotes him, at all but 15,000 of 90,000; and the German parliament's research service, which reports 35,000 to 100,000 before and 14,000 to 25,000 after, and 7682 prisoners dead in the camps. adjudications.claim: To all intents and purposes the appropriation of territory took place at the conference.
adjudications.reasoning: The Act names no Power's territory and the British government said territorial claims were not on its agenda, so the claim is contradicted as a matter of text; but Article I bounds a basin by watersheds and parallels in which the Powers' rules run, and Articles 34 and 35 lay down how future possessions on the coasts will be recognised, which is what Uzoigwe means by the appropriation being implied. Two producers, both European: qualified, and the position's own 'in the most technical sense' concedes the text.

restsOn.text:
HC Deb 20 November 1884 vol 294 cc57-8
MR. JACOB BRIGHT
asked the Under Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, If he has seen the following statement from the London Correspondent of The Manchester Guardian , and if there is any truth in it:—
It is, I understand, finally decided that our representative at the forthcoming Conference on the Affairs of the Congo at Berlin shall he instructed to support with firmness the claims of Portugal, which had been practically conceded before the Conference was proposed?
LORD EDMOND FITZMAURICE
Her Majesty's Government must decline at present to give any information in regard to the instructions given to their Representatives; but I have already stated that the decision of territorial claims is not among the bases of the Conference.
MR. JACOB BRIGHT
What I wish to ask is this—Whether the noble Lord is not aware that the proposition for conceding the Sovereignty of the Congo to Portugal has been all but universally condemned in this House and in the country?
LORD EDMOND FITZMAURICE
I am aware that considerable hostility was manifested, both in this House and "elsewhere," towards the Treaty of last year.
MR. ARTHUR ARNOLD
asked whether, if the Conference at Berlin should arrive at any conclusion on this subject, it would be laid before this House before it was accepted?
LORD EDMOND FITZMAURICE
No, Sir; I am not aware that it would.
SIR HERBERT MAXWELL
May I ask whether it is true, as reported in The Times this morning, that a Committee of Experts has been appointed to arrange the details of the agreement; and, if that is the case, can the noble Lord say to whom the interests of Great Britain are to be entrusted?
LORD EDMOND FITZMAURICE
I cannot undertake from day to day to give information of the proceedings of the Conference, and for this reason—that a pledge of secrecy has been given by all the Powers in regard to those proceedings; and if I were to depart from the rule of this House in one particular I should be obliged to depart from it
from day to day, until I had departed from it altogether.

adjudications.claim: Article 35's requirement of authority sufficient to protect existing rights was the doctrine of effective occupation, and Article 34's notification rule the doctrine of spheres of influence.
adjudications.reasoning: Article 35 says what Uzoigwe quotes it as saying, Article 34 is the notification rule he names spheres of influence, and both are confined to the coasts; the British government's answer of 20 November 1884 shows the conference was understood in London as rule-making. Two producers.

adjudications.claim: The great majority of African rulers chose to defend their sovereignty.
adjudications.reasoning: Three rulers speak in this record and all three defend a sovereignty: Witbooi tells Maharero he has given his land and his right of government into the hands of the white people, Lobengula tells the Queen he has not given away the whole country, Menelik proposes that a French text be the witness between the parties because he cannot compare the English with the Amharic; Daniel Kariko's affidavit says the Herero chose war. Three rulers and one under-chief are not the majority the claim counts, so the claim is borne out for every ruler this record holds and untested for the rest: qualified. Four producers on three sides.

adjudications.claim: The concession Lobengula signed was read to him as containing his words and gave away more than he had granted.
adjudications.reasoning: The king's two letters say so, and the Crown's editor records that a concession was granted on 30 October 1888 and that the Company was chartered to use it 'so far as they are valid'. On October 15, 1889, Lord Knutsford, on a Petition signed by the two Dukes, Mr. Rhodes, Lord Gifford, and others, granted the Charter, by which the Company were empowered to use and retain the full benefit of concessions so far as they were valid, and to acquire, by concession or agreement, rights and jurisdictions for the purpose of government in the lands referred to, subject to the approval of the Secretary of State. He must now explain how this concession was obtained from Lobengula, for it appeared that he had always absolutely denied that he ever granted it on the terms which appeared on the face of the instrument. When Lobengula was told that he had granted a concession of this nature he sent two Indunas to the Cape, with orders (as could be seen on reference to the Blue Book) to discover, first, whether such a place as England existed; and next, whether, if they discovered that such a place did exist, there was such a person as the Queen of England; and if there was such a place and such a Monarch, they were to lay before her the following letter and to ask her advice on the subject:—
"To Her Majesty Queen Victoria, from Lobengula.
"Some time ago a party of white men came into my country, the principal one appearing to be a man named Rudd. They asked me for a place where they could dig for gold, and said they would give me certain things for the right to do so. I told them to bring it to me, and I would see what I would do. A document was read and presented to me for signature. I asked what it contained, and was told that in it were my words and the words of those men. I put my hand to it. About three months after I heard from other sources I had given the right to all the minerals in my country. I called a meeting of my Indunas and of the white men, and demanded a copy of the document. It was proved to me that I had signed away the right to minerals of the whole country to Rudd and his friends. I have since had a meeting of my Indunas, and they will not recognise the paper, as it contains neither my words nor the words of those who got it from me."

adjudications.claim: The German protection Maharero accepted in 1890 would cost him his land and his right of government.
adjudications.reasoning: Witbooi wrote it in May 1890 and repeated in June 1891 that the Germans said they protected the chiefs against other nations but seemed to be the man who wanted the land; fourteen years later the German commander's order told the Herero to leave the country, and a Herero under-chief swore that their people had been compelled to work on farms and flogged. The order is the German army's own record, the affidavit is a British one, the letters the chief's own: three producers agree, but the order and the affidavit describe 1904, not the terms of 1890, so the prediction is borne out by what followed rather than tested against the protection treaty itself, which is not held: qualified.

2. The Sentries

One means by sentries ( sentili , native word,
taken from the English) the black overseers, armed
with a muzzle-loading gun, who have the official
duty of directing the work of the natives in the forest and of preventing the devastation of the same by
the cutting of the rubber vines, but whose labours
for the greater part of their time, are limited to calling to the minds of the natives their obligations,
seeing to it that they go to the forest and accompany the gatherers when they come to the post.

Two kinds of sentries can be distinguished.

Amongst the overseers, some, who belong to the
personnel of the post and who are nearly always
strangers to the region, patrol the villages at the
time when the natives should be at work, and report
to the whites those who instead of being at work
are staying at home. Very often, in order to exercise a more complete control, they are detailed to a
special village where they permanently establish
themselves. These are the sentilis , strictly speaking. They are by far the worst sort. In their
quality as strangers, they are not interested in the
blacks with whom they deal.

This is above all because no exact figures on the size of the Herero people survive either for the time before the war or for the time after it. It will be interesting to reproduce the famous Amnesty Proclamation of von
Lindequist. .It is a document which speaks tellingly of what the treatment of
Hereros had been prior to its publication. |

When one considers the fate and treatment of these unfortunates who, ‘ like
broomsticks,” and so thin that ‘one could see through their bones,” came in and
surrendered to German “mercy,” it seems doubtful, in view of the aforegoing
statements, whether they would not have been as well off if they had remained to
perish of starvation in the bush.

The Proclamation, dated 1st December 1905, reads as follows :—

Hereros! His Majesty the Emperor of Germany, the high Lord Protector
of this Land, has graciously nominated me Governor of this Land a few days

after General von Trotha, who commanded the German troops against you,
returned to Germany. His departure means that the war will now cease.

Hereros! You know me! Formerly I was for five years in this land
as Imperial Judge, and, as Assessor and Councillor, the representative of
Governor Leutwein in the days when Manasse of Omaruru and Kambazembi
of Waterberg, who were always loyal supporters of mine, still lived.

It is my desire that the Rebellion which your Chiefs and Headmen (and
the children who followed them) so wickedly began and which has desolated
the land should now come to an end, so that Peace and Order may again rule.
I therefore call upon the Hereros who still are wandering about the veld and
in the mountains and who nourish themselves by eating wild roots and by
theft. Come and lay down your arms, Hereros! Thousands of your fellow
tribesmen have already surrendered and are being clothed and fed by the
Government. I have taken every precaution to ensure that you will be
justly treated. That I also personally guarantee to you. Further, it is
ordained that from 20th December onwards, that is three weeks from to-day,
no Herero habitations will be searched after and taken, as I wish to give you
time personally to come in peacefully to me and surrender yourselves. Come
to Omburo and Otjihaenena! Your Missionaries will be sent there by me.
They will also take provisions with them, so that your first and great hunger
may be appeased. Some small stock will also be left for provisional use of
your wives and children in so far as you still possess such for their support.
Those who are strong and can work will, when they work with exceptional
diligence, receive a small wage. No European soldiers will be stationed at
Omburo and Otjihaenena, so that you need not have fear and imagine that
further shooting will take place. The sooner you come in and surrender your
arms, the sooner can the question of amelioration of the present lot of your
captive fellow tribesmen be considered and their freedom later again given to
them. If Omburo and Otjihaenena are too far away, anyone may hand in
the arms at any Military Post and surrender there. The soldiers at those
stations will not shoot either. In addition, the soldiers escorting the transport
and travelling through the land will not shoot at you as long as you attempt
nothing hostile towards them. Therefore do not be afraid of them when you
see them. So come quickly in Hereros, before it is too late. In Namaland
also there will soon be quiet, as Hendrik Witbooi has been killed by a German
bullet and Samuel Isaac has surrendered and is in our hands.

. On. this Proclamation the surviving Hereros surrendered, and thousands of them
then met the fate already depicted at Luderitzbucht and Swakopmund and in the
Railway Concentration Labour Camps.

restsOn.text:
It will be interesting to reproduce the famous Amnesty Proclamation of von
Lindequist. .It is a document which speaks tellingly of what the treatment of
Hereros had been prior to its publication. |

When one considers the fate and treatment of these unfortunates who, ‘ like
broomsticks,” and so thin that ‘one could see through their bones,” came in and
surrendered to German “mercy,” it seems doubtful, in view of the aforegoing
statements, whether they would not have been as well off if they had remained to
perish of starvation in the bush.

The Proclamation, dated 1st December 1905, reads as follows :—

Hereros! His Majesty the Emperor of Germany, the high Lord Protector
of this Land, has graciously nominated me Governor of this Land a few days

after General von Trotha, who commanded the German troops against you,
returned to Germany. His departure means that the war will now cease.

Hereros! You know me! Formerly I was for five years in this land
as Imperial Judge, and, as Assessor and Councillor, the representative of
Governor Leutwein in the days when Manasse of Omaruru and Kambazembi
of Waterberg, who were always loyal supporters of mine, still lived.

It is my desire that the Rebellion which your Chiefs and Headmen (and
the children who followed them) so wickedly began and which has desolated
the land should now come to an end, so that Peace and Order may again rule.
I therefore call upon the Hereros who still are wandering about the veld and
in the mountains and who nourish themselves by eating wild roots and by
theft. Come and lay down your arms, Hereros! Thousands of your fellow
tribesmen have already surrendered and are being clothed and fed by the
Government. I have taken every precaution to ensure that you will be
justly treated. That I also personally guarantee to you. Further, it is
ordained that from 20th December onwards, that is three weeks from to-day,
no Herero habitations will be searched after and taken, as I wish to give you
time personally to come in peacefully to me and surrender yourselves. Come
to Omburo and Otjihaenena! Your Missionaries will be sent there by me.
They will also take provisions with them, so that your first and great hunger
may be appeased. Some small stock will also be left for provisional use of
your wives and children in so far as you still possess such for their support.
Those who are strong and can work will, when they work with exceptional
diligence, receive a small wage. No European soldiers will be stationed at
Omburo and Otjihaenena, so that you need not have fear and imagine that
further shooting will take place. The sooner you come in and surrender your
arms, the sooner can the question of amelioration of the present lot of your
captive fellow tribesmen be considered and their freedom later again given to
them. If Omburo and Otjihaenena are too far away, anyone may hand in
the arms at any Military Post and surrender there. The soldiers at those
stations will not shoot either. In addition, the soldiers escorting the transport
and travelling through the land will not shoot at you as long as you attempt
nothing hostile towards them. Therefore do not be afraid of them when you
see them. So come quickly in Hereros, before it is too late. In Namaland
also there will soon be quiet, as Hendrik Witbooi has been killed by a German
bullet and Samuel Isaac has surrendered and is in our hands.

. On. this Proclamation the surviving Hereros surrendered, and thousands of them
then met the fate already depicted at Luderitzbucht and Swakopmund and in the
Railway Concentration Labour Camps.

gaps.status: paywalled at the publisher; the SOAS repository was refused by the container's egress policy and its worktribe mirror answered a Cloudflare challenge. The position rests on the work as named
